Alvastra
AHL-vahs-trah
n. (the Swedish Cistercian abbey of 1143, the first in Sweden, where Birgitta of Sweden lived and claimed revelations)
Old Swedish Alvastra, from alver, elves, or a local root; latinised Alvastrum.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Alvastra in Östergötland was founded in 1143 and settled directly from Clairvaux, on the same day as Nydala, the two being the first Cistercian houses in Sweden. Its best-known connection is Birgitta Birgersdotter, later Birgitta of Sweden: her husband Ulf died at Alvastra in 1344, she stayed on in a house by the abbey for some years, and it was there that she began to dictate the visions published as the Revelationes, which she said were given her by Christ and the Virgin, and which carried political instructions to popes and kings. She founded the Bridgettine order and was canonised in 1391. The dictionary honours her courage in addressing the powerful and names the claim itself as the corruption. A revelation that arrives after the apostles is tested, not received, and the test is a written one, “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20), applied against a deposit already closed, “the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). The standard is set so high that no messenger whatever is exempt from it, “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you” (Gal 1:8), and Peter, who had seen Christ transfigured with his own eyes, still ranked the written word above that experience, “We have also a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19). Her courage may be honoured. Her visions may not be believed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a revelation as the act of disclosing what was before unknown, especially divine truth; a vision as something apparently seen otherwise than by ordinary sight; a visionary as one who is given to reveries; canonization as the act of declaring a saint; and the canon as the genuine books of Scripture.

expand to see more

REVELATION, n. The act of disclosing or discovering to others what was before unknown to them; especially, the direct communication of truth to men by God.

VISION, n. The act of seeing external objects; also, something imaginary; a phantom; a supernatural appearance.

VISIONARY, n. One who is given to reverie; one who forms impracticable schemes; one whose imagination is disturbed.

CANONIZATION, n. The act of declaring a man a saint, or of ranking a deceased person in the catalogue of saints.

CANON, n. In theology, the genuine books of the Holy Scriptures, called the sacred canon or rule of faith.

Isa 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

Jud 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

Gal 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

2Pe 1:19 — "We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:"

Modern Corruption

Sweden's first Cistercian house, 1143, where Birgitta of Sweden began dictating the revelations that founded the Bridgettine order.

expand to see more

Birgitta of Sweden told popes to return to Rome and kings to stop their wars, and the dictionary grants her the courage that took. What she claimed for her authority is the problem. The Revelationes are presented as the words of Christ and of the Virgin given directly to her, and that claim puts them where only one kind of writing stands. Scripture provides a test rather than a welcome, “if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

Rome canonised her in 1391 and still reckons such private revelations as worthy of belief though not binding, which concedes the principle while softening the edge. Scripture closes the deposit, “it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you” (Jud 1:3), and sets the standard so high that no messenger is exempt from it, “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you” (Gal 1:8). Peter, who had seen Christ transfigured, ranked the written word above that experience, “We have also a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew torah (H8451), law; Greek paradidomi (G3860), to deliver over; Greek anathema (G0331), accursed; Greek bebaios (G0949), sure, firm.

expand to see more

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, direction, instruction; “To the law and to the testimony”, Isaiah 8:20.

Greek hapax (G0530) — once, once for all; “which was once delivered unto the saints”, Jude 1:3.

Greek epagonizomai (G1864) — to contend earnestly; “earnestly contend for the faith”, Jude 1:3.

Greek anathema (G0331) — accursed, devoted to destruction; “let him be accursed”, Galatians 1:8.

Greek bebaios (G0949) — firm, sure, steadfast; “a more sure word of prophecy”, 2 Peter 1:19.

Usage

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the test a new revelation gets."

"“which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) — a deposit already closed."

"“though we, or an angel from heaven” (Gal 1:8) — no messenger exempted."
